A classical ideal pictures knowledge as a market for ideas, where we weigh competing claims and let the best facts shape our beliefs. That would be the scientist's way, at least in theory. In practice, however, most of the time we are shopping in a market for justifications. We choose words not because they carry ideas, but because they carry stories about ideas. Often we are not really searching for facts to decide what we ought to believe. Usually we already know what we believe before we begin. What we are really after are statements that justify those beliefs, which is the lawyer's way.
①how scientists carefully test every idea against the evidence
②why the market for ideas always produces the truest beliefs
③how lawyers and scientists share the very same way of thinking
④how we usually look for words that justify beliefs we already hold
⑤why stories about ideas are more entertaining than facts

Imagine you have spent years working on a difficult technological problem. Suppose, too, that you have stayed alert to anything else you met that might relate to it. In that case, a creative solution may suddenly appear in your mind when you are relaxed. Such eureka moments, when great insights lead to discovery, often arrive at unexpected times. To encourage this kind of creativity, you must pay attention to things that could lead to valuable outcomes. This does not mean narrowing your interest down to a single topic. On the contrary, breadth of experience is the real key to creativity, while a narrow range narrows the imagination.

Shame is tied to who we believe we are, while guilt is tied to the things we actually do. We feel guilty when we measure a particular action against the kind of person we hope to become. That feeling is uncomfortable, yet it works in our favor. When someone apologizes, repairs the harm they caused, or drops a habit they dislike, guilt is usually the force behind the change. Guilt is every bit as strong as shame, but its effect tends to be constructive, whereas shame is frequently destructive. Research suggests that shame instead eats away at the very part of us that believes change is possible.

Scrolling through social media is a fast way to trigger dopamine in your brain. The moment you open the apps, you feel really good and your dopamine shoots up incredibly fast. But as the laws of physics remind us, whatever goes up must eventually come down. Your brain and body are always trying to return to balance, a state called homeostasis. So after dopamine spikes, your brain has to push it back down to restore that balance. It drops an equal amount below your usual level, leaving you feeling even worse than before you began.

George Bird Grinnell, one of the leading figures in early American conservation, was born in New York in 1849. Growing up near Audubon Park, he developed an early interest in birds. After graduating from Yale University, he joined his first scientific expedition, which led to his career in conservation. From the late 1870s, he wrote many articles in Forest and Stream calling for wildlife conservation. He helped found early conservation organizations, including the Audubon Society, and supported the establishment of Glacier National Park in 1910. Through his writings and public campaigns, he influenced the making of early wildlife protection laws. Even after his death in 1938, his work in conservation continues to inspire conservationists.

Our world is not merely interconnected; it is constantly changing, even when we fail to notice it. While you read these words, you yourself are changing, aging just a little and reshaping the neural networks in your brain. Even when you seem to be doing nothing important, distant events are quietly unfolding that will alter your life later on. The ancient Greek philosopher Heraclitus put it well: no one ever steps into the same river twice, for neither the river nor the person stays the same. His student Cratylus pushed the idea further, insisting that we are not simply onlookers watching the flow. When we step into the river, we stir it and reshape it, so we are agents who help make the change happen.

Describing what something smells like is the most basic way to talk about our sense of smell, yet even this turns out to be hard. English offers no words that capture smells the way "blue" or "green" capture colors. Instead, we describe a smell by naming its source, calling things "flowery," "fruity," or "fishy." Even familiar odors are hard to identify once they are taken out of their usual setting. In one study, most people could not name very common smells such as beer, roses, or motor oil. Yet anyone would happily drink the beer while refusing the motor oil, which shows that we react to smells correctly. Evolution has shaped our brain so that we respond well to odors through action but are poorly equipped to put them into words.

The major difference between working memory and long-term memory is one of awareness. We are consciously aware of what sits in working memory, but we cannot reach into long-term memory directly. Instead, we pull information out of long-term storage and into working memory in order to use it. For instance, you are not now picturing every actor you have ever watched on screen. Those memories rest in long-term storage, well outside your consciousness. Yet if asked to name them, you would draw them, one by one, into working memory and recite them. Working memory makes this possible, though it can hold only about seven items at a time.

Every day we step into the world and quickly judge what is safe and what is appropriate. According to psychologist Joseph LeDoux, an unconscious "danger detector" decides whether something or someone is safe before our conscious mind even gets started. If that detector labels an object or person as dangerous, the so-called "fight or flight" fear response is triggered at once. We may correct the detector's mistakes when we consciously notice them, but more often we simply invent reasons for why it was right all along. Although we are sure our choices are purely rational, most of our decisions are actually made by emotion first, and only afterward do we gather facts to justify them. By the time something merely "feels" dangerous, we have already begun to act inside before any real thinking has taken place.

A viewfinder is a piece of card with a hole cut through it in the middle, which can be used to isolate a part of a picture or object. It allows us to concentrate on one small part or area without being distracted by the whole of what can be seen. Talking about what something smells like is the most basic way of talking about our olfactory experience, and even this most basic way of talking about smells is challenging. There are no words in the English language to describe smells in the same way in which "blue" or "green" describe colors. Instead, to talk about how something smells, we talk about the source of the odor. Things smell "flowery," "fruity," or "fishy." Furthermore, even the most familiar odors are difficult to identify when they are not experienced in their usual context. In one experiment the majority of participants was unable to name very common odors like beer, urine, roses, or motor oil. Obviously, even those who couldn't name any of these odors would drink the beer but not the urine or the motor oil. This is how evolution has shaped our brain: We respond to odors correctly in many different ways, but we are not well-equipped to talk about them.

The big difference between working and long-term memory is that we are explicitly aware of the information in working memory, but we are not able to directly access the information in our long-term memory. We access long-term memory by bringing the information into working memory. For example, right now you are not aware of all the actors you have ever seen. They are stored in your long-term memory outside your consciousness. However, if I asked you to list all the actors, you would use your working memory to retrieve them one by one and reel them off. Your working memory can access your long-term memory and bring those memories to awareness. But remember it has a limit of seven items or chunks. Each actor would be an item. If you gesture while describing an event, do you think you'll be able to recall that event better than if you don't gesture? We had adults watch videos of toy objects, animals, and people performing various, sometimes odd, actions: a chicken sliding to a policeman, a jogger bending down to touch his toes, a fence swinging shut on its own. We then tested the adults' memories of these events immediately after the descriptions and three weeks later. Adults who were told to gesture while describing the events remembered more than adults who were told not to gesture, particularly several weeks later. To see if we'd get the same effects if people gestured on their own, we did the study again, but this time we gave the adults no instructions about gesture. We found the same patterns: people remembered items on which they had gestured spontaneously better than items on which they had not gestured. We go out in the world every day and make decisions about what is safe or not and what is appropriate or not. It is what psychologist Joseph LeDoux has suggested is an unconscious "danger detector" that determines whether or not something or someone is safe before we can even begin to consciously make a determination. When the object, animal, or person is assessed to be dangerous, a fear response, which has been called "fight or flight," occurs. On a conscious level we may correct a mistake in this "danger detector" when we notice it, but often, of course, we simply begin to generate reasons for why it was accurate in the first place. We are generally convinced that our decisions are "rational," but in reality, most human decisions are made emotionally, and then we collect or generate the facts to justify these decisions.
